text: Of David. Vindicate me, LORD, for I have walked in my integrity; I have trusted in the LORD; I will not be shaken.

versions.text: Of David. Vindicate me, LORD, for I have walked in my integrity; I have trusted in the LORD without wavering.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two distinct clauses: a statement of trust and a confident declaration ('I shall not slip/waver'). Collapsing them into an adverbial phrase loses the forward-looking confidence of the second clause and flattens the parallel rhythm of the line.

text: Examine me, LORD, and test me; refine my heart and mind.
For your steadfast love is before my eyes, and I walk in your truth.
I do not sit with deceivers, nor keep company with hypocrites.
I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked.
I wash my hands in innocence and walk around your altar, LORD,
lifting my voice in thanksgiving and telling of all your wonders.
LORD, I love the house where you dwell, the place where your glory abides.
Do not sweep away my soul with sinners, nor my life with men of blood,
in whose hands are wicked schemes, whose right hands are filled with bribes.

versions.text: whose hands are full of scheming, whose right hands are filled with bribes.
versions.explanation: The verb 'full' (מָלְאָה) belongs only to the second clause; the first simply says 'in whose hands is a wicked scheme.' Repeating 'full' in both clauses adds content and makes the couplet redundant.

text: But as for me, I walk in my integrity; redeem me and be merciful to me.
My foot stands on level ground; in the assemblies I will bless the LORD.

versions.text: My foot stands on level ground; in the great assembly I will bless the LORD.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew noun is plural ('congregations/assemblies'); 'the great assembly' introduces an adjective not present in the text and obscures the plural.
